title: The US is about to make its allies pick a side in the AI cold war
excerpt: A leaked State Department letter warns 35 partner nations they cannot belong to both American and Chinese AI initiatives, turning the Pax Silica pact into a loyalty test.
content_html:
Washington is preparing to hand its partners an ultimatum, and it is not a subtle one. According to a draft State Department letter reported by Reuters, the US is about to tell friendly nations they must choose between the American and Chinese artificial intelligence ecosystems, because belonging to both is no longer an option.

The letter is addressed to the 35 countries that signed a June “AI Opportunity Statement”, and its language is unusually blunt for a diplomatic cable. “To be part of everything is to be part of nothing,” the draft reads. “Signature of the Pax Silica Declaration is not merely a membership subscription, but a commitment.”

The mechanism doing the work here is Pax Silica, an initiative launched last year to lock down supply chains for AI models, semiconductors and critical minerals.

The carrot is access to shared AI investment opportunities reserved for members. The stick is exclusion for any country that also signs up to China’s competing framework. It is leverage dressed as a club membership.

Roughly two dozen nations have joined so far, including Japan, Australia and South Korea. Only one country, Kazakhstan, currently sits inside both the American and Chinese coalitions, which is less surprising once you remember it is a significant source of the critical minerals everyone wants.

That awkward overlap, one foot in each camp, is precisely the kind of arrangement the letter is designed to end, and Astana may soon find its hedging position untenable.

One US official put the reasoning plainly. “It’s difficult to see how a country can credibly position themselves as trusted partners in one technology ecosystem while simultaneously signing up for an initiative designed by China to advance a competing vision for AI,” the official said. The subtext is that neutrality now reads, in Washington, as a form of defection.

The timing is not accidental. Cheap Chinese open-weight models have been steadily eating into the market once owned by proprietary American systems, and a cheap Chinese model is now closing in on Anthropic and OpenAI on both cost and capability. When your commercial lead is narrowing, geopolitics starts to look like a handy substitute.

China, for its part, has stopped playing defence. In July, Xi Jinping launched a rival “World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization”, built explicitly around open-weight technology and open to anyone who wants in.

It is the mirror image of Pax Silica, and its openness is the whole pitch. Beijing is even weighing curbs on overseas access to its best models, a sign of how much leverage it now thinks it holds.

For anyone who lived through the last decade, the choreography feels familiar. This is the Huawei-era 5G pressure campaign, restaged for large language models, with allies once again asked to rip one vendor out of the stack and commit to the other.

Not everyone in Silicon Valley thinks that works. Mark Zuckerberg has argued the US should not block Chinese AI models at all, on the grounds that bans tend to backfire.

Europe, predictably, is caught in the middle. The bloc has spent years insisting on “strategic autonomy”, the polite European term for not having to choose between Washington and Beijing. Being handed a signature line and told to pick a side is exactly the corner it hoped to avoid, and the draft letter offers no obvious room to wriggle.

The State Department, for the record, declined to comment on what it called “purportedly leaked internal documents”, which is diplomatic code for confirming very little while denying nothing.

The letter may yet be softened before it is actually sent. But the direction of travel is clear enough: the AI cold war has quietly acquired a loyalty test, and for America’s partners the comfortable era of hedging your bets is drawing to a close.

content_html_zh:
华盛顿正准备向其合作伙伴发出最后通牒，而且这并不是一个微妙的最后通牒。 据路透社报道的国务院信函草稿，美国即将告诉友好国家，他们必须在美国和中国的人工智能生态系统之间做出选择，因为不再选择同时属于这两个生态系统。

这封信是写给 6 月份签署“人工智能机会声明”的 35 个国家的，其语言对于外交电报来说异常生硬。 草案中写道：“成为一切的一部分就等于什么都不是。” “签署 Pax Silica 宣言不仅是会员资格，更是一种承诺。”

在这里开展工作的机制是 Pax Silica，这是一项去年发起的计划，旨在锁定人工智能模型、半导体和关键矿物的供应链。

胡萝卜是获得为会员保留的共享人工智能投资机会。 大棒是对任何也签署中国竞争框架的国家的排斥。 这是伪装成俱乐部会员的杠杆。

到目前为止，已有大约二十几个国家加入，其中包括日本、澳大利亚和韩国。 目前只有一个国家哈萨克斯坦同时属于美国和中国的联盟，一旦你记住它是每个人都想要的关键矿产的重要来源，这就不足为奇了。

这种尴尬的重叠，即每个阵营一只脚，正是这封信旨在结束的安排，阿斯塔纳可能很快就会发现其对冲地位站不住脚。

一位美国官员将理由说得一清二楚。 这位官员表示：“很难想象一个国家如何能够将自己可靠地定位为一个技术生态系统中值得信赖的合作伙伴，同时又签署了一项由中国设计的倡议，以推进人工智能的竞争愿景。” 潜台词是，在华盛顿，中立现在被解读为一种叛逃形式。

这个时机并非偶然。 廉价的中国开放重量模型一直在稳步蚕食曾经由美国专有系统拥有的市场，而廉价的中国模型现在在成本和能力上都在接近 Anthropic 和 OpenAI。 当你的商业领先优势缩小时，地缘政治开始看起来像是一个方便的替代品。

就中国而言，它已经停止防守。 今年 7 月，习近平发起了一个竞争对手“世界人工智能合作组织”，该组织明确围绕开放重量技术建立，并向任何想要加入的人开放。

它是Pax Silica的镜像，它的开放性是整个球场的。 北京甚至正在考虑限制海外获得其最佳车型，这表明它现在认为自己拥有多大的影响力。

对于任何经历过过去十年的人来说，编舞都会感觉很熟悉。 这是华为时代的 5G 压力运动，为大型语言模型重新上演，盟友再次被要求将一个供应商从堆栈中剔除并转向另一个供应商。

并非硅谷的每个人都认为这有效。 马克·扎克伯格认为，美国根本不应该阻止中国的人工智能模型，因为禁令往往会适得其反。

不出所料，欧洲陷入了夹缝之中。 多年来，欧盟一直坚持“战略自主”，这是欧洲的礼貌用语，指不必在华盛顿和北京之间做出选择。 被递给签名行并被告知选择一方正是它希望避免的角落，而且信件草稿没有提供明显的回旋余地。

据记录，美国国务院拒绝就其所谓的“据称泄露的内部文件”发表评论，这些文件是确认很少但不否认任何内容的外交规则。

在实际发送之前，这封信可能还会软化。 但前进的方向是足够明确的：人工智能冷战已经悄然接受了忠诚度考验，对于美国的合作伙伴来说，两面下注的舒适时代即将结束。
